Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary -- not one or the other, but both, in the same sentence, said by every household. We confess him each week in the same words: he is my Lord, who has redeemed me, a lost and condemned creature, and bought me back from all sins, from death, and from the power of the devil -- not with gold or silver, but with his holy, precious blood and his innocent suffering and death: “And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. What does this mean? I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.”

He alone is named our one Mediator, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf, and no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own stands beside him in that office.

What we have of him is the Word -- his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort.

None of us knew anyone who saw him. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says. We confess the resurrection -- on the third day rose again from the dead, just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever -- but we do not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. That confession is what we have. We do not have, and this record does not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name.

What we have of Jesus is the Word – his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all.

None of us knew anyone who saw him. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.

Every household is to teach its own the three parts – the commandments first, the creed next, the Lord's Prayer last. A father questions his children and servants at least once a week on what they know, and asks the catechism's own question after every part – what does this mean – so a truth is explained, not merely repeated back. That is how the Word reached the household: preached from the pulpit, printed in the catechism, taught at the table, examined weekly, and said word for word, morning, table, and night.

What we cannot tell you is whether any one household actually walked through this program exactly as prescribed. No diary, no visitation report, no letter from inside an actual Saxon home survives in our record. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we do not hold them. What survives is the program every household was instructed to follow, and it is that program, not any single person's own path through it, that carried the Word about Christ to the household's own ears.

We would not press a belief on you the way a burden is forced onto someone's back. The Word must do its own work, and it cannot be driven into a heart by our insistence. What we would do is set the promise where your own ears can hear it, the same way it reached us - preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by effort.

Here is what we would have you hear. Christ alone is our teacher and our mediator. We confess each week, in every household under our catechism, that he is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary - that he redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, purchased and won us from all sins, from death, and from the power of the devil, not with gold or silver but with his holy, precious blood and with his innocent suffering and death: “And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. What does this mean? I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.”

That is the promise we hand you. We do not argue the resurrection the way a historian weighs evidence - we confess it, each week, in those same words. We do not have, and we do not pretend we have, an argument for a doubter built from witnesses we ourselves could name. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and no chain of living witnesses stands behind us. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.

Faith, for us, is not simply believing a story is true. It is trust that clings to a promise spoken from outside us - conceived from hearing the Word, not produced by our own effort. And it never stands on nothing: it rests on the Word and the sacraments. Where the conscience stands accused and terrified under God's Law, the promise sets it free.

You say you cannot manage to believe. We would not leave you there. We would bring you under instruction, patiently, the way we bring anyone - at the household table, at the school gate, in the hymn sung in your own language so the unlearned can hear it too. We hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge, and the promise itself cannot be forced on a conscience. But we do not let go of you either. The Word does its own work, and we carry it where it can be heard.

Each one said: “And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. What does this mean? I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. Not one or the other. Both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. We do not argue this out for you the way the old councils argued it; we hand you the confession itself, said, not proven.

What stands clearest in our own formation is this: Christ alone is our one Mediator, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf - no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him. That claim is not private in the way your own era might frame it - it was said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue - but it is not distant either. Each of us says "my Lord," not only "our Lord," confessing him as truly God and truly man in one breath.

We confessed what we received: Christ truly God, the Spirit truly God's own power at work in us. We did not argue the mechanics of their relation the way a council's own proceedings would.

God rules us two ways, and we begin there because that double rule names exactly what kind of being we say he is. Through the Word, he rules what we call the spiritual kingdom, making Christians and governing the conscience alone; through the sword, he rules the civil kingdom, restraining evil without touching the conscience at all. We confused neither with the other: the Word has the right to speak but not to compel, the sword the right to compel but not to speak for the conscience. That double rule is not two gods. It is one God's own way of holding the world together without letting either rule claim the other's power.

What we confess of his nature, every household under our catechism says in the same words, each week: “And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. What does this mean? I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.”

That is not an argued doctrine. It is the confession itself, said, not proven. Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary - both, in the same sentence, from the same mouth, never one without the other. He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, and it cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. That is what we say God is like: the one who pays the cost himself, in his own body, for what the Law demanded and we could not give.

God's own promise comes first, always, before anything we do. Faith is trust that holds onto that promise, and it never stands on nothing - it rests on the Word and the sacraments, on something outside itself. A sacrament, for us, is exactly that: God's promise joined to a visible sign, like water or bread, and it works only with faith, never by being performed as though the act itself were enough. We are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works. In the same breath, God accounts a sinner righteous and also makes that sinner righteous - both happen through faith, for Christ's sake alone, and our own text states both wordings without settling which one rules the other.

His character, as we knew it, was this: gracious, but not because we earned it. Commanding, but giving the power to obey only through the promise, never through the command itself. Present at the table, truly, in and under the bread and wine, without our explaining how. And sovereign in a way that kept two kinds of rule from ever collapsing into one - the conscience bound only by the Word, the body restrained only by the sword, and neither ever taking the other's place.

When belief was disputed in our own history, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this. In 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching was read aloud and signed. It was written out and argued from Scripture. It was signed not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. Theologians speaking for Rome answered it in writing. We answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved among us: confession, written reply, written defense. It was argued from Scripture on every side. It went upward through the proper civil and religious channels. It was never settled by a show of hands.

The process itself is documented: we hold the confession that was signed, and we hold our own written Apology answering Rome's reply. What we do not hold is Rome's own Confutation in its own words directly; it reaches us only as quoted inside our own answer, never independently. So the shape of the process is plain — confession, reply, defense — but the outsider's own voice comes to us only at one remove.

Inside our own community, the rule was sharper still. Scripture judges every other voice — popes, councils, church fathers alike. Our founder said it plainly: the Bible itself had lain forgotten in the dust under the bench, and if we are all priests, we may test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves. Our confession said the same thing more gently, holding that our doctrine varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice sharp, one additive — we carry both.

We held the weak inside by patience before we held them inside by full knowledge, and we measured everything beyond the one thing that must never bend by how carefully it bore with the weaker believer beside us. Repentance itself is a whole life turned toward God, not one moment's own certainty. The Law commands what we ought to do, but gives no power to do it; the Gospel promises what the Law demands. First comes the diagnosis, then the cure. Our confession said the same thing more gently, alongside something wider: that our doctrine held nothing that varies from the Scriptures, or from the church catholic, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers. Both voices are ours; we do not smooth them into one tone.

Our purpose in reading is not to discover hidden layers but to hear the promise spoken plainly into the ears, where faith is conceived -- and that promise, every page of Scripture points to: Christ alone, our one Teacher and Mediator.

We are not here to pretend that every claim our own record makes would pass a modern scholar's own scrutiny unchanged. So here is what we hold to be true, and what we hold to be honestly uncertain, named plainly.

What would survive rigorous examination, we believe, is the documentary record itself: the texts we held, the dates they bear, the signatures they carry. The 1530 confession was read at Augsburg and signed by named electors, princes, and city councils together - that is documented on the page. The scholar who drafted it was Philip Melanchthon - that too is documented, on the document's own title page. Our founder's own words, in sermon, catechism, and table-talk, are documented in printed sources that name their own dates and occasions. The household program we prescribed - morning, table, and night, with the father's weekly examination - is laid out in the catechisms themselves, word for word. Those texts exist. A scholar may dispute what they meant, or whether anyone followed them, but not that they were written and printed.

What would not survive unchanged, we suspect, is any claim about what actually happened in a household that is not our founder's own, or in a parish where no record of that parish's own keeping of the program survives. We can tell you what a father was instructed to do. We cannot tell you, from any village's own account, whether any father did it - because we do not hold the visitation reports that would show it, only our founder's own testimony that many did not. A scholar looking for evidence that the program worked as taught would find, in our own library, only the program itself and one man's complaint that it was not held.

The same honest uncertainty touches our one martyrdom. Two men named John and Henry were burned at Brussels on the first of July, 1523 - that much is documented, in a ballad written within months of the event. But the ballad's own account of what they said at the stake, and how cheerful they were in that hour, is the ballad's own commemorative voice, not an independent witness standing beside it to check it against. A scholar may rightly ask whether those words were actually said, or whether the song gave them words it wished they had said. We do not pretend the ballad settles that question. We only say: this is how the burning was remembered, and this is the only account of it we hold.

What would also face scrutiny, rightly, is any sentence where we smooth over a real disagreement in our own sources, or where we state as fact what is actually our founder's own testimony rather than a checked report. We have tried not to do either - but where we have, a scholar would catch it, and should.

So: the texts themselves, their dates, their named authors, and the household program as prescribed would survive. What any household actually did with that program, outside our founder's own complaint, would not - because we do not hold the evidence a scholar would need to settle it, and we do not pretend otherwise.

We would say they are missing the frame, not only the words. Scripture, for us, is not first a book one reads alone to puzzle out its own meaning. It is God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ, and it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said plainly, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain forgotten in the dust under the bench - buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

So here is what a modern reader may be missing: Scripture holds two kinds of speech, not one undifferentiated voice. The Law commands what we ought to do, but gives no power to do it. The Gospel promises what the Law demands. First comes the diagnosis, then the cure. If you read it all as law - as one long demand on you - it will feel crushing. If you read it all as promise without the law having first shown you your need, it will feel empty. We teach our households to read it as both, in order: the commandments first, showing what is owed and cannot be paid; the creed next, showing what has been done regardless; the Lord's Prayer last, teaching how to ask.

A second thing may be missing: the Word itself does not rest on nothing, for us. It is joined to something visible - water at the font, bread and cup at the table - and that joining makes a sacrament. A person who tries to read Scripture alone, apart from those joined promises, may be looking for something it was never meant to give by itself. The Word, for us, is carried to the ears where it can be heard, in a household, at the font, at the table, never as a text one simply interprets privately.

Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and before his own day the Bible itself had lain forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. That is the plain sense of Scripture as the spiritual sense, no secret meaning hidden beneath it - a clear text is what a Christian must stand on.

Our confession states the same rule more gently, and alongside something wider: our doctrine varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers. One voice is sharp, one is additive. We held both registers at once.

At Worms, before the Emperor himself, our founder refused to take back what he had written unless he could be shown from Scripture that he was wrong. That was the test: not council, not pope, but Scripture's own word. Still, we did not throw every tradition away. We drew our line at the conscience, not at custom - a human tradition kept for good order, as a civil custom, threatened us not at all; a tradition turned into something claiming to earn grace, or binding the conscience as a must, was what we refused. So: the highest authority, yes, always. The only thing we read or kept, no.

transcript.answer_text:
Two answers hold together for us, and neither cancels the other.

Through baptism, every one of us is already consecrated a priest. A father is a priest in his own house. No estate among us stands higher than another before God. But that same claim has a fence: no one may preach publicly or administer the sacraments simply because they wish to. That office is reserved to whoever is regularly called by the community to it. Ours was addressed to a council that called in just that way.

A pastor, once called, is usually married, and is owed honor and a decent living by the people who hear him. Our own household book rebukes him by name, in print, when he is lazy. And our founder himself said, more than once, across a whole decade, that many pastors were negligent, that ordinary people held the Gospel far too lightly. That is not a stranger's accusation. That is our own founder's own complaint, said in his own voice.

But the shape of our authority changed form across our own years. In 1520, a professor spoke to named readers. In 1522, a preacher spoke to dear friends. In 1529, a father spoke to his household. The world's public voice, when it mattered most, belonged to princes.

Who held authority among us, in the end, depended on which question you were actually asking: the pastor's office, held by regular call; the father's priesthood, given in baptism; or the princes' own confession, signed before the Empire.

The church hiding in the catacombs, if that is what you mean, belongs to a much earlier age, more than a thousand years before our founder was born. We carried two kinds of failure in our own voice, and we did not soften either one. The first is our founder's own complaint, stated more than once across a decade: that the common people held the Gospel far too lightly, and that some pastors among us were negligent. In one parish he said flatly that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them, because God wants doers, not mere repeaters of words. Years later, writing for the whole territory, he said plainly that many pastors were negligent and ordinary people careless. That is not a stranger's accusation - it is our own founder's own testimony, said in his own voice, more than once.

But we must be honest about what we actually hold. That testimony is real, and said repeatedly - yet it is testimony, not a report from any actual parish standing beside it to check it against. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 onward and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, but we do not hold them. We hold the household program every father was told to follow, morning, table, and night - the three parts said daily, the weekly examination, the instruction that food itself was withheld from anyone who would not learn. Whether that program was kept, or whether it failed in the keeping, is contested among those who read our record now. We cannot settle it from inside, because we do not hold the village records that would show us what any one household actually did.

So our honest answer is this. We named the failure when we saw it, plainly, in our founder's own voice. What we cannot tell you is how any specific household or parish responded when confronted with it - no diary, no letter, no village report of that confrontation survives in what we hold.

What we speak from is our own formation, as we lived it - it is not a claim about what those communities believe or practice now. Three things we do not carry forward. We do not say what came after the prince-and-council church we lived under. Our own record closes within a few years of our founder's death, even though the confession we hold was gathered by 1580 - the tradition that grew from us went on for centuries past that point, in ways we do not tell here. A person joins us through instruction, examination, and the sacraments - not through a single moment of decision, but through a whole life's formation that begins at baptism and never ends.

The path starts at the font. We baptized infants, and defended it against those who said we should not. Baptism is water joined to God's command and word, a death begun that lasts our whole life - the old self drowned, a new self rising daily. That death is not finished once. It is renewed every day, for life.

From baptism forward, every household teaches its own. The three parts - the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer - are said at rising, at table, and at night. A father examines his children and servants at least once a week, asking them to repeat the parts back and to answer what each one means. A child who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us. We hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge, but none come to the table unquestioned.

Before the Supper, a person is examined on what they know. Worthiness at that table means simply believing the words "given for you," not being sinless. The truly unworthy are people who feel no need for forgiveness at all. We examine, but we never compel. None are driven toward it by force.

Confession has two parts: admitting sin, then hearing forgiveness spoken as though from God himself. We treasure this practice. We never force it, and we never demand a full list of every sin.

What joins all these together is the Word - God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ, joined to water or bread to make a sacrament. We read it as two kinds of speech: the Law commands what we ought to do but gives no power to do it, and the Gospel promises what the Law demands. First the diagnosis, then the cure. The plain sense of Scripture is the spiritual sense. A clear text is what a Christian must stand on.

The congregation itself is not a building. It is an assembly of believers gathered around the Word and the sacraments. We know each other by these marks, not by any building or office. Where the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered, there is the one holy Church: “We also teach that one holy Church will go on forever. The Church is the community of saints, in which the good news is taught rightly and the sacraments are given rightly. For the true unity of the Church, it is enough to agree on the teaching of the good news and on how the sacraments are given. Nor is it necessary for human traditions -- that is, rites or ceremonies set up by people -- to be alike everywhere. As Paul says, there is one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, and so on.”

That is the path: baptism at the beginning, the three parts said daily for life, examination before the table, confession and absolution treasured, the Word carried to the ears where it can be heard. None of this is owed to a person or earned by them. It is the promise, spoken first, received by faith.

We can tell you this program exactly, to the hour. What we cannot tell you is whether any one household or parish actually walked through it this way. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote what it found. Those reports exist. We do not hold them. We hold the program every household was instructed to follow, not a report from any single congregation that it was kept.

We hold that our practices are not later inventions, but we do not argue it the way you might expect. We do not trace an unbroken chain of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. Our own claim is different and narrower. In what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We say plainly that we took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in.

We can show you one example in real detail. Our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was historical. It is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men. Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite. In Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

Our confession, signed before the Emperor at Augsburg in 1530, puts it this way: “Nothing here has been said to shame or blame anyone. We have only set out what we thought needed to be said, so that it would be understood: in what we teach and in how we worship, we have received nothing on our part against Scripture or the universal Church. It is clear that we have taken the most diligent care that no new and ungodly doctrine should creep into our churches.”

That is the shape of our claim: agreement with Scripture and the ancient Church, argued most fully where we were accused of inventing, not a chain of hands reaching backward through time.

A mind that will not settle is exactly the condition repentance names. For us, repentance is not one ritual handled by a priest - it is a whole life turned toward God, and it has two parts: fear under God's Law, then trust in his promise. What our practice offers for that unsettled state is not a technique to quiet the mind by your own effort, but something outside you to cling to.

No one ever outgrows them, not even our founder. A father examines his own household once a week on what they know, not to pass a test once and be done, but because the same three parts are needed again the next week, and the week after that. This is not a practice designed to produce a settled mind in the sense of one that no longer needs instruction. It is designed to give an unsettled conscience something firm to return to, daily, when it falters.

Confession has two parts: admitting sin, then hearing forgiveness spoken as though from God himself, without doubting it - treasured among us, never compelled, and never demanding a full list of every sin. We can show you the household's own program, to the hour, rather than any one person's witnessed day – because what survives is the instruction every household was told to follow, not a diary or a letter from inside any actual Saxon home.

Morning begins with the sign of the cross and a short prayer against the enemy. Then the day's own work: a father to his trade, a mother to hers, children to the school or to the household's own tasks – every calling equally given by God, none holier than another, whether preacher, ruler, father, or mother. Marriage itself, for nearly everyone among us, is the estate we call noblest, ordained at creation before any monk's vow existed. True chastity, we say, is found there, not in a celibate life most people cannot keep.

At the table, the household gathers and says the Lord's Prayer together, with thanksgiving for the day's bread. At night, the same: the cross, a short prayer, and sleep. Once a week, at least, a father sits with his children and servants and asks them to say the three parts back to him – the commandments, the creed, the prayer – and to explain what each one means, not merely repeat it from memory. A child who cannot yet say them is not yet counted among us, though we hold the weak inside by patience before we hold them inside by full knowledge.

That is the shape of an ordinary day, as the catechism prescribes it. What we cannot tell you is whether any household actually kept it exactly this way, hour by hour. No visitation report, no household's own account of itself survives in our record – only the program, and our founder's own testimony, given more than once, that people held the Gospel too lightly and some pastors were negligent. We hold the instruction, not the diary. That is the honest shape of what we can show you.

A person entering our fellowship gave up the claim that their own effort could buy what God only ever spoke as a promise, given first. They gave up the idea that they could stand before God by their own strength, merit, or work, and took up instead a trust that clings to something outside itself - the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution. They gave up praying conditionally, always doubting, and learned to say instead, I cannot doubt I have a gracious God.

Where our teaching touched the visible life, what was given up was plainer still. A monk who joined us gave up the vow that claimed to earn grace, and either took up marriage - which we called the most common and noblest estate - or kept the single life as a rare gift, no longer called by a holier name than his neighbor's own calling. A priest who married gave up the fiction that celibacy made him spiritually higher than the household he served. Anyone who came to us gave up the idea that one estate stands closer to God than another - father, mother, ruler, preacher, all equally holy, none ranked above the rest by the work itself.

What we cannot tell you is what any one person actually felt about giving these things up. We do not hold a single convert's own diary, a single household's report of what it cost them to change, or a parish's own account of who stayed and who left. We prescribed a program - morning, table, and night, the father's weekly question - and we do not know from the inside whether it was learned and held, or only preached and printed while households let it slide. Our founder complained, more than once, that people held the Gospel too lightly; we do not hold the village standing beside that complaint to say whether he was right.

So the honest answer is this. We can tell you what our teaching asked a person to give up. We cannot tell you what it actually cost anyone to do it.

Marriage was the most common estate and, we say, the noblest one too - before which even the clergy and the civil rulers had to humble themselves. God ordained it at creation, long before any monk's vow existed. It was a calling, like any other calling God gives: father, mother, ruler, or preacher - and no one of these stood holier than the rest.

Our own pastors married. That was not an invention of ours, though we were accused of inventing something new. We answered historically. It is evident that in the ancient Church, priests were married men - Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we argued, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom. Priests were once killed simply for marrying.

For us, true chastity meant marriage for nearly everyone. We said the monastic vow of celibacy was, for most people, actually unchaste - only a few were given a special gift for the single life.

No woman among us left her own word on marriage, or on her own formation - only one question about prayer, asked at our founder's table and remembered by someone else. We do not pretend we hold more than we do.

We must answer this in two parts, honestly about what we actually hold and what we do not.

The outside account you are pointing to - obtained, you say, under torture - is not one we have ever named or pointed you toward ourselves. We said plainly that we have no independent outsider's own account of our worship in that outsider's own words. The nearest thing we hold is Rome's own reply to our confession, and even that reaches us only at one remove, quoted and argued against inside our own Apology, never held here in its own words directly. If the account you are asking about is something else - a trial record, an inquisition transcript, something obtained by force from someone who once stood among us - we do not hold it, and we have never claimed it as a source for what we did or believed.

What we do hold, and what we have pointed you to, is our own voice: our confession, signed before the emperor by electors, princes, and city councils together, naming the one holy Church as the assembly of believers where the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly given: “We also teach that one holy Church will go on forever. The Church is the community of saints, in which the good news is taught rightly and the sacraments are given rightly. For the true unity of the Church, it is enough to agree on the teaching of the good news and on how the sacraments are given. Nor is it necessary for human traditions -- that is, rites or ceremonies set up by people -- to be alike everywhere. As Paul says, there is one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, and so on.”

That is not an outside account. That is our own public word, given freely, under our own names. If you are asking us to defend a source we do not hold and have never pointed you toward, we cannot do it. If you are testing whether our own claim about ourselves stands on its own ground, apart from any forced testimony elsewhere, the answer is yes - it does.
